subsection: 3. The provision of education in Ireland

notes.b: Pre-school (early childhood) education is provided by private, community and voluntary services before a child starts primary school. It is not compulsory, but it gives children a head start, so the State funds some of it.
points: The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) scheme provides a free pre-school year to children before they enter primary school, delivered through approved providers. It is a government scheme, so it costs families nothing.

Early Start is a one-year preventative pre-school programme for three- and four-year-olds, run in selected primary schools in disadvantaged areas. It aims to give children a positive start and prevent later school failure.
Early Start is staffed by primary teachers working with a child care assistant, so the programme is led by trained teachers.
The Access and Inclusion Model (AIM) supports children with disabilities to take part in the free pre-school programme, so they are not left out.
Naíonraí are pre-schools where children learn through the Irish language.
Montessori schools, which are generally privately run, use trained teachers and encourage children to learn through play at their own pace.
Playschools give children of a similar age the opportunity to play together and learn to share, take turns and follow group rules.
Pre-school builds language, social skills and the routines a child needs for the transition to primary school, so children settle in more easily when they start.
notes.tip: If asked for one government scheme that supports pre-school, name ECCE or Early Start and say what it provides and who it is for. For Early Start, say it is for children in disadvantaged areas.

notes.b: Primary school is the first stage of compulsory education. Exams ask for the ages involved, the types of school to choose from and the alternatives open to parents.
points: Children may enrol in primary school from age four and must begin by age six, because school is compulsory from six.
Primary education is an eight-year cycle, from junior infants to sixth class, and most pupils finish between the ages of 12 and 14.

Primary schools are state-funded or private. A state-funded school is paid for by the State but run by its patron (the religious body, Educate Together or other group that runs it), so it is not state-run and not private.
State-funded schools may be religious, multidenominational or non-denominational. Educate Together is an example of a non-denominational school, and it is not a private school.
Specialist types include Educate Together schools, Gaelscoileanna (Irish-medium schools, where subjects are taught through Irish), Montessori schools and single-sex schools.
Parents may educate a child at home instead of enrolling them in a school. Home-educated children are registered with Tusla.
notes.tip: For a primary education question, cover the age range (enrol at four, begin by six, eight years), the types of school and the choice open to parents.

notes.b: Second-level education follows primary school and is made up of several programmes. Each has a set length, a particular kind of curriculum and its own form of assessment, which is how exams ask you to describe them.
points: Junior Cycle is a three-year programme that uses classroom-based assessments and ends with a state examination at the end of third year, marked by the State Examinations Commission. Its award is the Junior Cycle Profile of Achievement, which replaced the old Junior Certificate.

Transition Year is an optional year between Junior Cycle and Leaving Certificate with no state examination. It focuses on personal development, work experience and self-directed learning (students taking charge of their own learning).
The Leaving Certificate Programme is a two-year programme that ends with state examinations at the end of sixth year.
Leaving Certificate subjects are offered at higher and ordinary level, and foundation level exists only in Irish and mathematics. Grades are converted to points for third-level entry.

Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) is a two-year modular programme (made up of separate units) with practical, written and oral assessment. It suits students who prefer practical learning and can lead to Post Leaving Certificate courses.
The Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (LCVP) has two link modules: Preparation for the World of Work and Enterprise Education. Work experience is part of Preparation for the World of Work.
notes.tip: When asked to name and describe a programme, give its name, what it covers (subjects or modules) and how it is assessed. Do not mix up Transition Year (optional, no exam), LCVP and LCA.

notes.b: Work experience is a placement in a workplace. It lets a student try out working life while still at school, and the benefits are a common exam question.
points: Work experience is part of the Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (inside the Preparation for the World of Work link module) and is a standard element of Transition Year.
A placement lets students test their career preferences and see what a job actually involves, so they can make a better choice about their future.
Students learn workplace co-operation and how working life differs from school.
Work experience develops communication, teamwork, planning, organisation, punctuality and problem solving.
Students learn the expectations of a workplace, including timekeeping, appearance and health and safety.
Completing a placement builds confidence and responsibility, and gives the student a work record for a curriculum vitae.
notes.tip: Exams ask for benefits of work experience, so give separate, named benefits such as career clarity, teamwork, punctuality, confidence and a record for a CV, each with a short explanation.

notes.b: Third level is education after second level. It includes degree courses in colleges and further education courses, and students need a way in and a way to pay.
points: Third-level institutions include universities, technological universities and institutes of technology, which offer full-time degree and diploma courses. TU Dublin, created under the Technological Universities Act 2018, is an example of a technological university.
Most full-time undergraduate places are allocated through the Central Applications Office (CAO) using Leaving Certificate points, which are based on the grades a student earns.

Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses are full-time further education courses, usually delivered by Education and Training Boards in second-level schools and colleges. They provide training with work experience and can give access to third-level courses.
The Student Universal Support Ireland (SUSI) scheme provides means-tested grants (based on family income) towards the costs of approved third-level courses.
The Free Fees Initiative pays tuition for eligible undergraduates, so students pay only a student contribution.

The Higher Education Access Route (HEAR) and the Disability Access Route to Education (DARE) are reduced-points entry routes for students from disadvantaged backgrounds or with disabilities, so these students can enter with fewer points.
notes.tip: Do not confuse PLC courses (further education) with third-level degree courses. If asked for reasons for the rise in third-level participation, give separate reasons such as affordability, the value of qualifications for well-paid work, wide course choice and access schemes like SUSI, HEAR and DARE.

notes.b: Adult and second-chance education lets people return to learning at any age, whatever their earlier educational level.
points: Adult education courses are available full-time, part-time, modular, day, evening and weekend, and by distance learning, so adults can fit study around work and family.
Second-chance education gives people who left school early a route to qualifications, such as Youthreach.
Education and Training Boards (ETBs) run adult, community and further education courses; they replaced the Vocational Education Committees in 2013.
SOLAS, the Further Education and Training Authority, funds and co-ordinates further education and training programmes across the country.
Adult literacy schemes provide basic reading, writing and numeracy courses for adults.
Adult education builds skills for work, supports career change, and helps adults keep pace with new workplace technology.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain what adult and second-chance education means, to describe the provision, and to give reasons why adults return, such as better job prospects, career change and keeping up with technology.

notes.b: Students with special educational needs are supported through a combination of planning, specialist staff and school settings. The aim is that each student gets the help that suits their need.
points: An Individual Education Plan (IEP) sets out the goals, teaching approach and supports for a student with special needs, drawn up with the school and the parents.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) plans and co-ordinates special educational provision, and Special Educational Needs Organisers allocate supports to schools.
Special Needs Assistants (SNAs) provide care and support in class for students who have care needs or who need help to take part in lessons.

Special education teachers (formerly called learning support and resource teachers) give withdrawal teaching, taking students out of class individually or in small groups, to students with learning difficulties.
Special classes in mainstream schools, such as autism classes, have a reduced number of pupils per teacher, so each pupil gets more attention.
Special schools provide for students with significant general or specific learning difficulties, physical disabilities, or sensory impairments.
Visiting teachers advise and support students who are blind or vision impaired, or deaf or hard of hearing, and the teachers who teach them.
Assistive technology, such as text-to-speech software, helps students with reading or writing difficulties.
notes.tip: For a question asking you to evaluate supports, give several supports, say what each does and who it is for, and add a sentence on whether it meets the need.

notes.h: Other professional help and exam accommodations (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Beyond the school, specialist professionals assess needs and provide therapy, and the examinations themselves are adjusted for students who need it.
points: Educational psychologists assess students' needs and recommend supports, which helps the school decide what help to give.
The Health Service Executive (HSE) provides speech and language therapy and occupational therapy to children with special needs.

The State Examinations Commission provides reasonable accommodations in state examinations, such as a reader, a scribe or extra time, so that a student's disability does not stop them showing what they know.

keyTerms.definition: Early childhood education provided before a child starts primary school, including Montessori, playschool and Naíonra provision.

keyTerms.term: Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) scheme
keyTerms.definition: A State scheme providing a free pre-school year to children before they enter primary school.
A pre-school where young children learn through the medium of Irish.
The first three years of second-level education, which use classroom-based assessment and end with a state examination.
A two-year modular second-level programme with practical assessment that can lead to Post Leaving Certificate courses.
A full-time further education course, taken after the Leaving Certificate, that provides training with work experience and can give access to third-level courses.
The body through which most applications for full-time undergraduate courses are made in Ireland.
A public body that runs second-level, further education and adult education services in its area.
A written plan that sets out the goals and supports for a student with special educational needs.
A staff member who supports students with care needs or who need help to take part in class.

questions.prompt: Outline three types of pre-school provision available to young children in Ireland.
questions.model: Any three, two marks each: the Early Childhood Care and Education scheme, a free pre-school year before primary school; Early Start, a one-year preventative programme for three- and four-year-olds in selected disadvantaged areas; Naíonraí, Irish-medium pre-schools; Montessori schools, which use trained teachers and learning through play at the child's own pace; playschools, where children of a similar age learn to play, share and take turns.

questions.prompt: Discuss the provision of second-level education in Ireland, referring to Junior Cycle, Transition Year and the Leaving Certificate programmes.
questions.model: Junior Cycle: three-year programme with classroom-based assessments and a state examination at the end of third year, marked by the State Examinations Commission. Transition Year: optional year between Junior Cycle and Leaving Certificate, no state examination, personal development, work experience and self-directed learning. Leaving Certificate Programme: two years, state examinations at the end of sixth year, subjects at higher, ordinary and foundation levels, grades converted to points for third-level entry. Alternative senior cycle routes: Leaving Certificate Applied, a modular programme with practical assessment leading to Post Leaving Certificate courses; LCVP, which adds three link modules (enterprise education, preparation for work and work experience) and assesses a portfolio and a written exam. Each programme should be described for its curriculum and its assessment.
